title: QuIC Whitepaper Calls for Industrial Scale-Up Infrastructure in EU Chips Act 2.0 - Quantum Computing Report
gist: The European Quantum Industry Consortium says the EU Chips Act 2.0 proposal lacks industrial-scale paths for quantum fabrication, as IBM (Anderon, HRL) and IonQ (SkyWater) fold foundries into US quantum companies. It asks for strategic-project status, subsidized MPW shuttles, cryogenic and packaging infrastructure and visible/UV photonics support.

themes.theme: Foundry consolidation by US quantum players

insights.claim: IBM is committing over $10 billion to quantum initiatives, including establishing Anderon, a pure-play quantum wafer foundry supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce, and acquiring HRL Laboratories.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Quantum leaders are vertically integrating into fabrication with state backing, shifting the moat from qubit design to manufacturing access.

insights.claim: IonQ completed its acquisition of SkyWater Technology, the largest exclusively U.S.-based semiconductor foundry and an accredited Category 1A Trusted Foundry for U.S. defense programs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A quantum company owning a defense-trusted foundry blends quantum, chips and defense procurement, a distinct competitive position.
insights.quote: IonQ completing its acquisition of SkyWater Technology, the largest exclusively U.S.-based semiconductor foundry

insights.claim: QuIC argues that deals folding neutral semiconductor foundries into vertically integrated quantum companies threaten European supply-chain resilience.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Neutral foundry capacity is being absorbed by competitors, which could squeeze non-integrated quantum hardware firms.
insights.quote: consolidate neutral semiconductor foundries into vertically integrated quantum companies

insights.claim: Most European quantum hardware firms rely on neutral process foundries rather than owning fabrication plants, so their access to commercial-grade quantum fabrication rests on voluntary, revocable terms set outside the Union.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: European quantum hardware valuations carry a hidden dependency on foreign foundries that could be withdrawn.
insights.quote: European access to commercial-grade quantum fabrication currently rests on voluntary, revocable terms set outside the Union
insights.locator: Because most European quantum hardware firms

insights.claim: QuIC says the Chips Act 2.0 proposal (COM(2026) 504) recognizes quantum chips and six EU pilot lines but lacks dedicated mechanisms for industrial-scale manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The policy gap is between prototyping and production, so funding may favor shared infrastructure over a single large foundry.
insights.locator: While QuIC welcomed the continued recognition

insights.claim: The six EU quantum pilot lines cover superconducting (SUPREME), spin (SPINS), photonic (P4Q), diamond (DIREQT), neutral-atom (Q-PLANET), and trapped-ion (CHAMP-ION) modalities.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The EU is spreading pilot-line support across six modalities rather than picking a winner.
insights.locator: While QuIC welcomed the continued recognition

insights.claim: QuIC wants Article 19 strategic-project status extended to quantum foundries, so a legal framework exists when quantum manufacturing reaches industrial maturity.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Strategic-project status would open fast-track support for the first European quantum foundry.

insights.claim: QuIC proposes a subsidized European multi-project wafer shuttle calendar to give quantum startups and SMEs affordable shared fabrication access, as a route to capacity without an immediate multi-billion-euro foundry.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shared MPW access would favor small quantum startups, a cheaper alternative to building a foundry.
insights.quote: To build sustainable European fabrication capacity without requiring a multi-billion-euro foundry immediately
insights.locator: To build sustainable European fabrication capacity

insights.claim: QuIC asks that Chips Act photonics goals extend beyond near-infrared telecom wavelengths to visible (400 to 800 nm) and deep-UV (295 to 325 nm), which trapped-ion and neutral-atom architectures need.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Existing photonics baselines are built for telecom, leaving ion and atom modalities without matching fab process support.

insights.claim: QuIC calls for shared cryogenic testing, characterization and advanced packaging facilities across 2 K, 4 K and millikelvin ranges, plus cryogenic PDKs and assembly libraries.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cryogenic packaging and test are named bottlenecks, pointing to demand for equipment and services in that niche.

insights.claim: QuIC wants the Chips Act 2.0 (chip-level fabrication and PDKs) aligned with the upcoming EU Quantum Act (systems, software, standards and public procurement).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The EU Quantum Act is a second policy lever, and public procurement rules could shape demand for European systems.
insights.quote: QuIC also called for structural alignment between the Chips Act 2.0
insights.locator: QuIC also called for structural alignment
